answers.answer: The client sends to the service entry point; the reverse proxy forwards to a selected application backend, which performs the operation and sends the response through the balancer back to the client. Choose L7 for /search and /purchase pools: it must read HTTP contents, so an HTTPS proxy normally terminates client TLS; encryption onward to the backend is separately configured. L4 typically selects for the TCP connection using network information, not paths. Many requests reuse that connection and can all stay on its chosen backend without further selections. One adequate server can suffice if neither traffic distribution nor redundant serving is needed.

evidence.quote: The balancer forwards the request to a selected backend, which performs the operation and returns a response through the balancer to the client.
Many HTTP requests can reuse that connection. They can all reach the same backend; adding requests on that connection does not force new selections.
Path routing requires readable HTTP contents.
Understands HTTP requests. It can route /images and /reports to different backend groups, or select a backend for each request.
One adequate server may be enough if the service does not need traffic distribution or redundant serving.

answers.answer: Round robin takes turns among eligible backends, counting a cheap lookup and a long request equally; equal counts can hide unequal work. Least connections prefers fewer active connections and is worth considering for long, uneven work, but connections can carry very different amounts of work. Weights control traffic share: twice the measured capacity could start at twice the weight, but static configured weights neither measure live capacity nor guarantee performance. Check latency and resource use to choose. Another API backend supplies API capacity but does not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck, so throughput may remain limited by that database. After failure, clients need a reachable alternate entry path through an available managed entry or redundant frontends with tested working failover. Surviving backends need enough spare capacity for redirected load; otherwise limit or visibly reject excess work rather than assuming redistribution suffices.

evidence.quote: a quick read and a slow report still each count as one request.
Prefers the backend with fewer active connections. This can help when connection durations vary, but one connection may carry far more work than another.
A server with twice the measured capacity might start with twice the weight. Configured weights are not a live measurement or a performance guarantee.
More API servers can help when API processing is the bottleneck; they do not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck.
After one backend fails, the survivors need enough capacity for the remaining load.
Use an available managed entry or redundant frontends with working failover, and test that path.

answers.answer: A 200 from a process health endpoint does not show that the purchase handler can do useful work when its required database is inaccessible. The check should reflect capabilities required by application requests, including that dependency. Even improved checks sample periodically with limited coverage and failure thresholds, and a backend can fail immediately after passing, so detection is delayed. Once detected and removed from eligibility, it receives no new selections. Removal cannot finish, undo, or safely replay already running requests, which may still fail. The product all-unhealthy policy also matters: some send traffic to unhealthy targets if all fail checks.

evidence.quote: Readiness means it can accept useful new work: a process can answer /health while an application handler cannot reach its required database.
Checks have limited coverage, intervals and failure thresholds; a backend can fail just after passing. Detection takes time.
Once detected and removed from eligible backends, it stops receiving new selections. Requests already underway can still fail; removal does not complete, undo or safely replay them.

answers.answer: If the cart exists only in A memory, B cannot read it on the later request. If A fails the only cart copy can be lost. Stickiness prefers A for the same user and can keep ordinary requests where the cart exists, but may skew load and restrict placement. It does not copy the cart or preserve it when A fails. Shared session storage lets either backend read the cart, at the cost of access or coordination work and dependence on shared storage availability. Consistent routing and making state available elsewhere are separate duties.

evidence.quote: If a server keeps a user's session only in A's memory, B cannot read it. Losing A can lose the only copy.
It can keep ordinary requests on A, but skew load and restrict placement. It does not copy the session or preserve it when A fails.
Lets either backend read the session. It adds access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability matters too.

answers.answer: First stop new assignments to A; let the already accepted 20-second request finish within a bounded drain deadline, then shut A down after completion or deadline expiry. Accepted work remains on A while new assignments must cease; if the deadline forces termination before completion, the request may be interrupted and its work is not automatically moved to B. Merely refusing new L4 connections leaves the reused existing connection able to carry new HTTP requests. A drain must manage existing connection lifetimes or stop further requests, and L7 draining must track already accepted requests. Thus drain behavior must account for whether routing/assignment is per connection or per HTTP request. The supplied material gives no exact configured deadline, so it does not establish whether this 20-second request completes before shutdown.

evidence.quote: During a deployment, draining stops new assignments to A while allowing in-flight work, meaning requests already underway, to finish within a deadline. Shut A down after completion or when that deadline expires.

Stopping new L4 connections does not stop new HTTP requests on existing connections. A drain must also manage those connection lifetimes or stop accepting further requests. L7 request-aware draining must still track already accepted work.
Forced termination at the deadline may interrupt unfinished requests. Their work is not automatically moved to B.

answers.answer: The purchase can remain committed even though the response is lost, so a timeout cannot tell the client whether it completed. A blind retry on B may apply the purchase effect again. Assign a stable idempotency key to the one logical purchase and reuse it on every attempt. Every backend must use a shared durable key/result record. In one database transaction, reserve the key uniquely, apply the purchase effect and record its result, committing all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without applying the effect again. Separate checking and writing can race or leave a crash gap. A fresh key would not identify the retry as the same operation; A-only memory cannot reliably protect a retry at B. Bound attempts and add delays because extra requests consume capacity and worsen overload. This is application duplicate protection, not a guarantee that retries succeed or a property the balancer provides automatically.

evidence.quote: A backend commits a write, but its response is lost. The client cannot tell whether the write completed. A blind retry on another backend can repeat the effect.
A stable ID for one logical operation, reused on every attempt.

All backends use a shared durable record of the key and result. In one database transaction, reserve the key uniquely, apply the effect and record the result; commit all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without applying the effect again. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a crash gap.
A new key per retry, or a key remembered only in one server's memory, cannot reliably protect retries elsewhere.
Bound retry attempts and delay them: extra requests consume capacity and can deepen overload.
